# Ironclad and steel warships (`ironclad_warship`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs cannon_artillery; helped by steamship_screw_propeller, puddling_wrought_iron, bessemer_steel, naval_gunnery_line_of_battle
- Core idea: Guns firing explosive shells set wooden ships on fire, so ships were given a belt of thick wrought-iron plate over timber backing and steam engines to carry the weight. An armoured ship is practically immune to a wooden fleet. A contest of gun against armour followed: heavier rifled guns in a few rotating turrets, steel armour, and finally the all-big-gun turbine battleship of 1906. Fleets became a measure of industrial capacity, and each new type made existing fleets obsolete, which drove naval arms races.
- Pitfalls:
  - Iron plates do not make a ship sink; a ship floats by displacing its weight of water, whatever it is made of
  - The iron cladding of the Korean turtle ships of 1592 is not in the contemporary Korean sources and is doubted
  - Armour high up without matching beam makes the ship unstable
  - Monitor and Virginia (1862) were not the first ironclads; France had armoured floating batteries at Kinburn in 1855 before launching the ocean-going Gloire in 1859
- History: east_asia: 1592 – Korean turtle ships with a covered, spiked deck (iron plating disputed); europe: 1820s – Paixhans' shell guns; 1853 – shells destroy a wooden Turkish squadron at Sinope; 1855 – French armoured floating batteries at Kinburn; 1859 – Gloire; 1860 – iron-hulled HMS Warrior; 1906 – HMS Dreadnought; americas: 1862 – USS Monitor against CSS Virginia, first fight between ironclads
- Read:
  - James Phinney Baxter, The Introduction of the Ironclad Warship (1933)
